label: prop:skein-coulomb-enhancement
title: Coulomb enhancement from electron-proton Skein crossings
html:
Proposition. Coulomb enhancement from electron-proton Skein crossings

Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a Descartes universe with substrate parameter q. Consider the beta decay \mathcal{N}(Z, N) \to \mathcal{N}(p\!+\!1, n\!-\!1) + T_{2,3} + \nu^{\sigma}. The emitted electron T_{2,3} crosses each of the Z = p + 1 proton strands of the daughter nucleus as it exits the Hopf link. The q-deformed wedge product \wedge_q (crossing asymmetry) assigns weight q to each positive electron-proton crossing. This produces a coherent product that multiplies the decay rate by the Skein-Coulomb enhancement factor:

  F_q(Z, E)
  = 
  \frac{2\pi\eta_q}{1 - e^{-2\pi\eta_q}}

The q-deformed Sommerfeld parameter is:

  \eta_q
  = 
  \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q)
  \cdot \frac{Z}{\beta_e}

The EM coupling projection is \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q) = q^{-1}/([9]_q \cdot [10]_q) (EM coupling projection). The velocity of the emitted electron is \beta_e = v_e / c.

Derivation. We evaluate the canonical action \mathfrak{S}_q (canonical action) on the full outgoing state \psi = T_{2,3} \cup \mathcal{N}(p\!+\!1, n\!-\!1). This decomposes as:

  \mathfrak{S}_q\big|_\psi
  = 
  \mathfrak{S}_q\big|_{\mathcal{N}}
  + 
  \sum_{j=1}^{Z} \mathcal{S}_{e\text{-}p_j}
  + 
  \mathfrak{S}_q\big|_{T_{2,3}}

The middle sum runs over all electron-proton crossings. Each crossing contributes a Skein weight \mathcal{S}_{e\text{-}p_j}(q) = q. This is a positive crossing between two like-charge constituents. The electron radial wave function picks up a phase e^{i\delta_\ell} at each proton. The phase shift is:

  \delta_\ell
  = 
  \arg \Gamma(\ell + 1 + i\eta_q).

We form the coherent product of Z such scattering amplitudes. We sum over partial waves \ell and integrate over the electron energy spectrum. This yields:

  |\psi_e(0)|^2_{\text{Coulomb}}
  = 
  |\psi_e(0)|^2_{\text{free}}
   \times 
  F_q(Z, E).

The decay rate is directly proportional to |\psi_e(0)|^2, the electron wave function at the nuclear origin. Thus, F_q multiplies the leading-order rate.
